job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Wendy Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at 6:40 to catch the bus into Hartwell, where I'm a junior auditor at Marlow & Pike, a mid-size firm. I graduated top of my accounting class last summer, and this is my fourth month. Most days I tick through client invoices and bank statements in spreadsheets, and a senior called Gareth checks my work. I like the puzzle of a number that doesn't match, but by 4pm my eyes hurt. I share a flat with two housemates, Jo and Priya, and my student debt sits there in the background.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let me read the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, it means nobody is losing sleep, and I'd say it at the Friday pub with my housemates. Honestly I'd add that the software the firm already pays for is enough for me. I've never touched the chat tools and I'd be happy for that to stay true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel relieved but not safe, because the firm's partners keep talking about margins. Even small time savings let them hire one fewer junior, and I'm the newest junior. My debt payments don't care whether AI is hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going exactly as I am, and I'd put £150 a month into my savings pot, which is about two months of rent right now. I'd also finish my first professional exam paper in the spring. I'd keep my head down and learn the sampling work properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, a bit dull, and honestly that's fine. I like knowing what Monday looks like. The only flutter is the rent going up in March.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill or worry in your own life would stay exactly the same even if nothing changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent and my loan repayment stay the same whether AI is hype or not, and they worry me more than any software. That's about £620 for my room and £90 for the loan, and Jo is moving out, so I'd have to find someone new to share with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much of your week is routine screen work that even a small change could touch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quite a lot, to be honest. Maybe half my day is matching things and ticking boxes, and even a small tool that does the ticking would shrink what a junior is for. I'd notice it first in how many of us the partners hire next autumn.

say: I'd tell friends this is **fine** and that nobody needs to panic.
I'd say the firm's existing software is **enough** for my work.
I'd say my union-minded mum was right to be wary of hype.
think: I feel relieved but not safe, because partners watching **margins** could hire one fewer junior.
My **debt** and rent don't care whether AI is hype.
Half my day is ticking boxes, so even small tools could touch it.
do: Keep **auditing** the same way and finish my first professional exam paper in spring.
Put **£150 a month** into savings, building towards three months of rent.
Look for a new housemate before **March** when the rent rises.
feel: **Steady** and a little dull, which is fine by me.
A flutter of worry about **rent**, not AI.
S0.quote: Rent and my loan repayment stay the same whether AI is hype or not, and they worry me more than any software.
fieldNote: Her fear is about **money**, not machines; the debt and rent shape everything.
Never uses AI tools, so she judges them from the outside.
Notices the **junior hiring** link without being prompted, which shows how close it feels.

steps.text: Finish the first professional accounting exam paper in the spring
Pay £150 a month into a rent safety pot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let me read the next one, called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say it's another change that the partners will use to cut costs, and I'd say so quietly to Priya. Online I'd say the people who save money from this should share it with staff. I wouldn't be shouting about it, but I'd sign anything our union circulated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think my job is the first target. Checking invoices, matching bank lines and filling in sample tests is exactly what the software does well. Top of the class doesn't help much when the work I'm best at, checking and matching, is the work the software does first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Gareth, my senior, to move me onto client calls and the judgement parts of the audit. I'd cut my spending by about £100 a month, mostly takeaways and the train trips home. And I'd finally try the firm's new tool, with a colleague next to me, because I'd rather learn it slowly than be told I'm behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in the chest. I'm not the type who jumps into new things, so I'm worried I'd be the slow one on the team. But I'd also be angry, because decisions about my job are made in a room I'm not in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Think of a task you did last week. Which part would software take over first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The sampling tests. Last week I spent two days drawing samples from a client's ledger and checking them against documents, and software could do that in an afternoon. What's left is talking to the client's finance manager and judging whether an explanation is believable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your manager do differently about hiring people at your level?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think they'd stop hiring the second-year class to replace people who leave. Gareth's group had four juniors and now has three, and nobody said why. The partners would call it efficiency, and I'd call it being left to carry more with less.

say: I'd say the savings from this should be **shared** with staff, not just partners.
I'd back anything the **union** circulated at work.
I'd tell Priya quietly that the firm is using it to **cut costs**.
think: I believe **checking** work is the first target, and top marks won't protect me.
I'm slow to take up new tools, and I fear being the **slow one**.
Decisions about my job get made in rooms I'm **not in**.
do: Ask Gareth to move me to **client calls** and judgement work.
Cut spending by **£100 a month** on takeaways and train trips.
Try the firm's new tool with a **colleague** beside me.
feel: A **tight chest**, and fear of being the slow one.
S1.quote: Top of the class doesn't help much when the work I'm best at, checking and matching, is the work the software does first.
fieldNote: Blames **employers** and shareholders, not the technology itself.

steps.text: Ask Gareth to move me onto client calls and judgement work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let me read the next one, called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a disaster waiting to happen and that governments should have been writing rules years ago. At work I'd be careful, because the partners might hold it against me. At home I'd say it out loud to my mum, who is a nurse and a union rep, and she'd say we need to organise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my career would be over before it begins. Entry-level accounting is the work the software eats first, and 2028 is when I'd be 24. I'd still owe most of my student debt, and I'd have nothing to show for the degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything I can live without and put every spare pound into savings, aiming for six months of rent. I'd also go to my mum's union branch and join the campaign for a proper income guarantee. And I'd ask my parents whether I could move back home for a year, which I hate to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. I lie awake working out how long my savings would last, which is about two months. I did everything right, the grades and two internships, and I'd still be 24 with debt and a degree for work that no longer exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Say it's the day the announcement is made. What do you tell the people close to you that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mum first, in her kitchen, and say I might be out of work by 2028. She'd say we'd manage, but I'd see her counting. I'd tell Jo and Priya later, because we'd have to decide whether we keep the flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only 2 years, what happens to the money you owe and the money you've saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay the loan down as slowly as the rules allow and keep the cash, because cash matters more than being debt-free if I lose my job. I'd cancel the exam course I paid £400 for, since a qualification for a job that may vanish feels like waste.

say: I'd say governments should have written **rules** years ago.
I'd say we need to **organise**, as my mum the union rep always does.
At work I'd stay **careful**, so the partners don't hold it against me.
think: My career could be **over** before it begins, since entry-level accounting goes first.
I'd still owe most of my **debt** with nothing to show for the degree.
It feels **unfair** because I did everything right.
do: Save every spare pound towards **six months** of rent.
Join my mum's **union** branch campaign for an income guarantee.
Ask my parents if I can **move back home** for a year.
feel: **Sick** and lying awake counting how long savings last.
**Betrayed**, since grades and internships may not matter.
S2.quote: I did everything right, the grades and two internships, and I'd still be 24 with debt and a degree for work that no longer exists.
fieldNote: The only scenario where she expects to **lose** her job.
Turns to her mother's **union** world for both comfort and a plan.
Would keep cash instead of paying debt, a clear sign of **fear** over thrift.

steps.text: Save every spare pound towards six months of rent
Stop takeaways, trips and subscriptions to protect cash
Join the union branch my mum belongs to
Ask my parents if I can move back home for a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let me read the next one, called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough that the government and firms have no excuse not to prepare. I'd press my union branch to ask the firm about a training guarantee. I'd also tell friends not to be calm about it just because it's a bit away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the middle of my twenties is when it lands, just as I'd start earning properly. I might have a promotion or two by then, but also the firm may have stopped hiring juniors altogether. It's the gap between those two things that scares me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my professional qualification by 2028 so I'm at least qualified before the crunch. I'd start a second pot of savings and stay in the flat share to keep rent low. And I'd force myself to learn the audit tools properly, which I've been avoiding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less sick than the two-year version, more of a steady dread. I have time to act, and I'm not sure I'm the sort who uses it well. I put things off when I'm scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes about your plan with 5 years instead of 2?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd change my five-year plan. No buying a flat, no big holiday, and I'd think about a master's in something that needs people judgement, like forensic accounting. With two years I'd only panic, but with five I can at least train, and the question is whether I'm the sort who does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who around you do you think sees this coming, and who doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of the older seniors don't see it. Gareth thinks it's the usual sales talk from software firms. The graduates in my cohort mostly talk about it like a game, and the one friend who does take it seriously is already studying data skills.

say: I'd say five years is no excuse for **doing nothing**.
I'd press my union branch to ask for a **training guarantee**.
I'd tell friends not to be calm just because it's **further away**.
think: I fear the firm stops hiring juniors just as I'd start to **earn properly**.
I know I **put things off** when I'm scared.
I might get a promotion or two, but not **security**.
do: Learn the audit **tools** properly, which I've been avoiding.
Look into a **master's** in forensic accounting.
feel: Steady **dread**, with time to act but doubts about using it.
S3.quote: With two years I'd only panic, but with five I can at least train, and the question is whether I'm the sort who does.
fieldNote: Time changes her from **panic** to planning, but she doubts her own follow-through.
Names the **seniors** as the ones who don't see it coming.
Qualification and a master's are her main **routes** to staying useful.

steps.text: Learn the firm's audit tools one evening a week
Keep paying into a second savings pot every month
Ask the union branch to push for a training guarantee

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let me read the next one, called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and that people my age should use it to organise and push for protection. I'd tell my housemates it's not a reason to relax. But I'd say it with some calm, because a decade is long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be more hopeful. By 2036 I'd be 32, probably a senior in the firm or somewhere else, and I'd have had time to move into the parts of finance that need judgement and trust. I still think the juniors who come after me are in trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start now with the professional qualification, then a master's part-time. I'd learn at least one AI tool a year, slowly, so I'm not the person who refuses. And I'd save enough for a deposit on a small flat, because owning something feels like a shield.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mixed. A bit lighter, because I can plan, and a bit guilty, because the next graduates won't have my head start. I worry about the ones coming after me more than myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With a decade, what would you start now that you wouldn't with 2 years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a small side thing, like doing tax returns for neighbours and my mum's friends. That keeps me close to people, which is where machines are weaker. With two years I'd have no time; with ten I can build a name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: At 32, what do you hope your working life looks like, and what could stop that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I hope to be a manager who trains juniors properly, but the firm could shrink to a handful of partners and software. Then nobody would need a middle layer at all.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift** that young people should use to organise.
I'd say we should push for **protection** for the juniors coming after us.
I'd tell housemates it's still no reason to **relax**.
think: By 2036 I'd be 32 and hopefully in work that needs **trust**.
I worry more about the **next graduates** than about myself.
Owning a small flat would feel like a **shield**.
do: Do the professional qualification, then a **part-time master's**.
Learn one **AI tool** a year, slowly.
Save a **flat deposit**, and do neighbours' tax returns on the side.
feel: **Lighter**, because there is time to plan.
A bit **guilty** about the juniors who follow me.
S4.quote: I hope to be a manager who trains juniors properly, but the firm could shrink to a handful of partners and software.
fieldNote: A decade turns her **dread** into a plan, but the worry shifts to others.
Her answers return to **unions** and shared protection every time.
The side-work idea of **neighbours' tax returns** is her own, practical hedge.

steps.text: Start a part-time master's after the professional exams
Learn one new AI tool at work each year
Save towards a deposit on a small flat
Do neighbours' and mum's friends' tax returns on weekends

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, easily. It's the only one where I lose my job before I've paid off anything, and I'd have no time. What would help is a proper income guarantee, retraining paid for by the firms that benefit, and a union that bargains over how AI is used in audit.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd say People tell my generation to be flexible, but flexibility is easy when someone else owns the firm. I'd like the partners and the shareholders to be the ones asked to adapt, not the 22-year-olds with a loan.

headlineQuote: People tell my generation to be flexible, but flexibility is easy when someone else owns the firm.
portrait: Wendy is a **22-year-old** junior auditor, top of her accounting class, living in a shared flat with student debt.
She is slow with new technology and has **never used** AI tools, which shapes her fear.
Her outlook is progressive, so she blames **employers** and shareholders and trusts unions and rules.
Her mood runs from steady unease to **alarm** if AGI arrives in two years, easing with more time.
biggestWorry: The **2028** scenario worries her most, because she would lose her job before clearing her debt.
whatWouldHelp: An **income guarantee**, retraining paid by firms that gain, and union say over how AI is used in audit.
